profsave.format: Line-oriented 'GstKey Value'. The app only rewrites keys that already exist in the file, never adds new ones, and always writes a timestamped backup first.
profsave.warning: Battlefield 6 must be fully closed before writing. The game rewrites this file on exit and will overwrite your changes.
profsave.scale_note: Settings carrying profsave_scale are stored in the file in different units to the ones the app displays. Reads divide by the scale, writes multiply.

esports.label: Esports
esports.goal: Maximum frame rate and the flattest possible frame times. Visual fidelity is spent freely.

competitive.label: Competitive
competitive.goal: High frame rate, but keep the visual cues that actually help you spot players.

balanced.label: Balanced
balanced.goal: The game looks like the game, at a frame rate that matches your monitor.

quality.label: Quality
quality.goal: Best image the hardware can hold at a stable 60+.

settings.label: Field of View
settings.note: Wider sees more but shrinks distant players and costs a few percent on both CPU and GPU because more of the world is in frame. 90 vertical is the common competitive choice. If you get motion sick, come down rather than up.

pros: See more of the flanks without turning
Less tunnel vision in close quarters
cons: Distant players occupy fewer pixels and are harder to spot
More world in frame costs both CPU and GPU
Can cause motion sickness

pros: Distant targets appear larger
A few frames back on both CPU and GPU
cons: Narrower peripheral awareness
Feels claustrophobic to anyone used to wide FOV

settings.label: Resolution
settings.note: Always native, always fullscreen exclusive if the game offers it. Reduce load with the upscaler, not by running a non-native resolution — a non-native signal is both blurrier and higher latency than DLSS/FSR Quality at the same cost.

settings.label: Display Mode
settings.note: Exclusive fullscreen bypasses the desktop compositor: lower latency, and it is a prerequisite for G-Sync/FreeSync behaving properly. Use borderless only if you genuinely need to alt-tab constantly. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Exclusive fullscreen bypasses the desktop compositor: lower latency
Prerequisite for G-Sync/FreeSync working properly
cons: Alt-tabbing is slower and can flicker

pros: Instant alt-tab, easier with a second monitor
cons: An extra composition step adds latency
VRR often does not engage properly

settings.label: V-Sync
settings.note: Off in-game in every case. With a VRR display, enable V-Sync in the NVIDIA/AMD control panel instead and cap frames below refresh — that combination gives you tear-free output without the latency of in-game V-Sync.

pros: Removes up to a full frame of input latency
Frame rate no longer locked to refresh divisors
cons: Screen tearing without VRR

pros: No tearing
cons: Significant added input latency
Frame rate snaps to refresh divisors when you miss the target

settings.label: Frame Rate Limit
settings.note: Computed from your monitor and your predicted frame rate. A cap that you can actually hold at all times beats an uncapped average — frame time consistency is what your hands feel, not the number in the corner.

pros: Flatter frame times, which is what your hands actually feel
Keeps you inside the VRR window
Lower GPU power draw, less heat and fan noise
cons: Gives up peak frame rate you might otherwise see

pros: Higher peak frame rate
cons: Frame times get spikier as the GPU hits its power limit
Above refresh with VRR on, you fall out of the VRR window

settings.label: Upscaling / Super Resolution
settings.note: Chosen from your GPU: DLSS on RTX, FSR on Radeon and older NVIDIA, XeSS on Arc. Below Quality mode, distant players start to smear during strafing — which is the exact target you care about. The app will not select Performance mode for you at 1080p.

pros: Large frame rate gain for a modest image cost
Frees GPU headroom you can spend on textures and effects
cons: Below Quality mode, moving targets smear during strafing
Thin geometry like fences and wires can shimmer

pros: Sharper native image, no reconstruction artefacts
cons: Costs the frame rate the upscaler was buying you

settings.label: Frame Generation
settings.note: Generated frames are not sampled from your inputs, so latency goes up even as the counter goes up. Never for competitive play. It is defensible only if you are already above ~60 real FPS and want to fill a high-refresh panel in a quality-first setup.

pros: Roughly doubles the number on the FPS counter
Smoother-looking motion on a high-refresh panel
cons: Generated frames contain none of your input, so latency rises even as FPS rises
Artefacts around fast-moving objects, i.e. players
Needs a solid real frame rate underneath or it feels worse, not better

pros: Every frame you see reflects your mouse input
No interpolation artefacts on moving players
cons: Lower FPS counter

settings.label: NVIDIA Reflex / AMD Anti-Lag
settings.note: On, always. It keeps the render queue short automatically, which is the same job RenderDevice.RenderAheadLimit does by hand. '+Boost' only helps if you are heavily GPU-bound and costs power; plain 'On' is right for nearly everyone.

pros: Keeps the render queue short automatically: measurably lower click-to-photon latency
Costs no image quality at all
cons: 'On + Boost' raises power draw for a marginal gain

pros: Marginally lower GPU power draw
cons: Longer render queue, higher input latency for no visual benefit

settings.label: Texture Quality
settings.note: Textures cost VRAM, not frames. If you have the memory, high textures are the closest thing to free image quality in the game. If you do not, you get texture pop-in and hitching, which is far worse than a slightly softer wall. Capped by detected VRAM.

pros: The cheapest image quality in the game if the VRAM is there: costs frames barely at all
Sharper surfaces at every distance
cons: Exceeding VRAM causes texture pop-in and hard hitching, which is far worse than a softer wall

pros: Frees VRAM, preventing the spill-to-system-memory stutter
cons: Visibly muddier surfaces
Gives back almost no frame rate, so only worth it if VRAM is genuinely short

settings.label: Texture Filtering
settings.note: Anisotropic filtering keeps ground textures sharp at a distance. It has been effectively free on every GPU made in the last decade. Max it regardless of preset. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Ground textures stay sharp into the distance
Effectively free on any GPU of the last decade
cons: A fraction of a percent of GPU time

pros: Almost nothing
cons: Blurry ground at an angle, for well under 1% frame rate

settings.label: Lighting Quality
settings.note: One of the three biggest GPU costs in the menu. Dropping it also flattens the scene, which cuts both ways for spotting players — less shadow noise to search through, but fewer contrast cues.

pros: One of the three biggest GPU savings available
Flatter image means less shadow noise to search through
cons: Scene loses depth and contrast cues that help read a doorway

pros: Richer, more readable lighting
cons: Among the most expensive GPU settings in the menu

settings.label: Shadow Quality
settings.note: The single most expensive setting here and it costs CPU as well as GPU, because shadow maps mean extra draw calls. Going Ultra to Low is routinely worth 15-25% frame rate. Caveat: shadows cast around corners are a genuine information source at Medium and above, and Low removes some of them.

pros: The single largest frame rate lever here: Ultra to Low is routinely 15-25%
Also saves CPU, because shadow maps mean extra draw calls
cons: Shadows cast around corners are genuine information, and Low removes some of them
Visible shadow shimmer and pop-in at range

pros: Stable, detailed shadows; more corner information
cons: The most expensive setting in the menu, on both CPU and GPU

settings.label: Mesh Quality
settings.note: Controls geometric detail and how aggressively distant objects drop to simpler models. This is a CPU setting more than a GPU one. Do not run it at Low: aggressive LOD makes player models at range change silhouette, which is worse than the frames it buys.

pros: Meaningful CPU saving, which matters on a CPU-limited machine
cons: Aggressive LOD makes distant player models change silhouette as they pop between detail levels
Objects visibly morph as you approach

pros: Stable silhouettes at range, no distracting LOD popping
cons: Primarily a CPU cost, via extra draw calls

settings.label: Terrain Quality
settings.note: Terrain tessellation and detail. Medium is a good stopping point — Low can visibly change ground contours, and on a shooter with prone players that matters.

pros: Solid GPU saving on open maps
cons: Ground contours flatten, which matters when prone players use them

pros: Accurate terrain shape and detail
cons: Tessellation is not cheap on older GPUs

settings.label: Water Quality
settings.note: Controls water surface reflections, wave tessellation and the quality of the underwater transition. Medium is a solid stop: screen-space reflections at High and Ultra look impressive in captures but are barely visible when you are running across a bridge. Low replaces the surface with a flat texture.

pros: Meaningful GPU saving on water-heavy maps
Flat water surface is less distracting as a moving reflection while you are aiming
cons: Low makes water look flat and plasticky — obvious on coastal or river maps
Screen-space reflections disappear below Medium

pros: More convincing wave shape and real-time reflections
Ultra adds higher tessellation density and accurate refraction
cons: Costs GPU on every map, not just water-heavy ones
The Ultra-over-High detail is rarely visible during a firefight

settings.label: Undergrowth / Vegetation Quality
settings.note: Expensive on vegetated maps, and lower settings thin out the grass that players hide in. Competitive players deliberately run this low. Be aware that this is the setting most likely to be flagged as an unfair advantage in an organised match — check your league's rules.

pros: Large saving on vegetated maps
Thins the grass players hide in
cons: This is the setting most likely to be treated as an unfair advantage in organised play - check your league's rules
Noticeably barer world

pros: Dense, natural-looking foliage
cons: Expensive, and it gives enemies more cover against you too

settings.label: Sky / Volumetric Cloud Quality
settings.note: Volumetric cloud simulation and atmospheric scattering quality. Low replaces the volumetric clouds with a flat skybox texture — the most visible sky downgrade. Medium gives you real 3D clouds at a sensible cost. Ultra adds a higher ray-march step count that makes cloud edges and internal shadowing sharper, which matters most in wide-open outdoor maps.

pros: GPU saving on every map — clouds are rendered regardless of whether you look up
A flat skybox is less of a distraction while you are aiming upward at a rooftop
cons: Low gives you a baked flat texture: no 3D cloud shape, no weather progression
Atmospheric gradients become static

pros: 3D volumetric clouds with visible density and internal shadow
Ultra adds real cloud-shadow projection onto terrain
cons: Volumetric rendering costs GPU time even when you are not looking at the sky
Ultra's improvement over High is mostly noticeable in a screenshot

settings.label: Effects Quality
settings.note: Explosions, smoke, particles and destruction. This is where your 1% lows go to die in a busy Conquest fight — it is a frame time setting far more than an average FPS setting. Lowering it also thins smoke, which is a real tactical difference.

pros: The biggest 1% low improvement available: this is where frame times collapse in a busy fight
Thinner smoke means you can see through contested areas
cons: Thinner smoke also means your own smoke cover works less well
Explosions and destruction look flat

pros: Full-bodied explosions, smoke and destruction
cons: Costs both CPU and GPU exactly when the fight gets busy, so it hits 1% lows hardest

settings.label: Post Process Quality
settings.note: Bundles bloom, depth of field quality and assorted screen-space effects. Low is a clean win for both frames and clarity.

pros: Clean GPU saving
Removes bloom and screen-space haze that wash out targets
cons: Image looks flatter and less cinematic

pros: Richer bloom and screen-space effects
cons: Costs frames to add glare over the part of the screen you aim at

settings.label: Decal Quality
settings.note: Bullet holes, explosion craters, blood, scorched surfaces and other persistent marks. This controls both the resolution of each decal projector and how many remain active at once before the oldest are retired. Low causes marks to pop off surfaces quickly, which can reduce visual clutter in a sustained firefight — but also makes it harder to read where fire is landing.

pros: GPU and CPU saving in a heavy firefight — many simultaneous decals add draw calls
Marks disappear faster, reducing visual noise after a sustained engagement
cons: Fewer active bullet holes: harder to read where shots have been landing
Destruction surfaces stay cleaner and look less worn than they should

pros: Persistent, crisp marks give you a shot-landing readout on walls and ground
High-resolution decals on destruction debris look convincing up close
cons: Many simultaneous decals add draw calls on both GPU and CPU
Cost spikes during heavy contact, exactly when frame headroom matters most

settings.label: Ambient Occlusion
settings.note: Contact shadowing in corners and under objects. Off is a few percent faster; SSAO is cheap and adds depth cues that help you read doorways. RTAO is a ray tracing feature and priced accordingly.

pros: A few percent GPU back
cons: Image flattens; prone bodies and corner geometry lose the contact shadowing that makes them readable

pros: Depth cues in doorways and under objects
SSAO is cheap for what it adds
cons: RTAO is a ray tracing feature and priced like one

settings.label: Ray Tracing
settings.note: Never for competitive play — it is a 20-40% frame rate cost for lighting you will not look at while being shot. Only offered in Quality preset, and only on a GPU with strong RT hardware and enough VRAM.

pros: Genuinely better lighting and reflections in screenshots
cons: 20-40% frame rate cost for lighting you will not be looking at while being shot
Extra VRAM for the acceleration structures

pros: The largest single frame rate gain available on an RT-capable card
cons: Lighting and reflections lose accuracy

settings.label: Motion Blur
settings.note: Zero in every preset. It costs GPU time to make moving targets harder to hit. There is no configuration in which this is the right call for multiplayer.

pros: Moving targets stay sharp instead of smearing
Small GPU saving
cons: Motion looks less cinematic

pros: Smoother-looking camera motion
cons: Costs GPU time to smear the fast-moving objects you are trying to hit

settings.profsave_note: Stored in PROFSAVE_profile as 0.0-1.0; the app shows and writes it as a percentage.

settings.label: Chromatic Aberration
settings.note: Colour fringing at the screen edges. Nearly free to render and purely negative for clarity. Off.

pros: Removes colour fringing at the screen edges, where peripheral movement appears
cons: Loses a filmic look

pros: Filmic lens look
cons: Blurs and colour-splits the screen edges for no gameplay benefit

settings.label: Film Grain
settings.note: Adds animated noise over the whole image. It fights your upscaler's temporal accumulation and hides distant movement. Off.

pros: Static image, no animated noise hiding distant movement
Stops the grain fighting your upscaler's temporal accumulation
cons: Loses a filmic look

pros: Filmic texture
cons: Animated noise masks distant movement and degrades upscaler output

settings.label: Vignetting
settings.note: Darkens the screen edges — exactly where peripheral movement appears. Off.

pros: Screen edges stay bright, where peripheral movement shows up
cons: Slightly less focused-looking image

pros: Draws the eye to the centre
cons: Darkens exactly the region where you notice flanks

settings.label: Lens Distortion
settings.note: Warps the image at the edges. Off.

pros: Straight lines stay straight at the edges
cons: Marginally less lens-like

pros: Camera-lens feel
cons: Warps the edges of the image

settings.label: Camera Shake
settings.note: Costs nothing to render, but it moves your crosshair for you during suppression and explosions. Minimum for anyone trying to win a gunfight. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Your crosshair stays where you put it under suppression and explosions
Costs nothing to reduce
cons: Explosions feel less weighty

pros: More visceral feedback
cons: The game moves your aim for you during a firefight

settings.label: HDR
settings.note: Only if you have a display that actually does HDR well (true local dimming or OLED). On a cheap 'HDR400' panel it washes the image out and can cost you contrast against dark backgrounds. Off for competitive regardless of the panel.

pros: Much wider contrast range on a display that genuinely supports it
cons: On a cheap 'HDR400' panel it washes the image out and costs you contrast against dark backgrounds
Adds a small GPU and VRAM cost

pros: Predictable SDR contrast, which is what most panels actually do well
cons: Gives up real HDR on a capable display

settings.label: Brightness
settings.note: Slightly above default lifts detail out of shadowed interiors. Push it much further and you crush the contrast that makes a player silhouette readable.

pros: Lifts detail out of shadowed interiors
cons: Push it far and you crush the contrast that makes a silhouette readable

pros: Deeper blacks and more contrast
cons: Players hiding in shadow become harder to see

settings.profsave_note: Stored in PROFSAVE_profile as 0.0-1.0; the app shows and writes it as a percentage.

settings.label: Mouse Sensitivity
settings.note: Never changed by this app. Your muscle memory is worth more than any setting in this list.

settings.label: Mouse Acceleration
settings.note: Off. Acceleration means the same physical movement produces a different in-game rotation depending on speed, which is the opposite of building muscle memory.

pros: The same physical movement always produces the same in-game rotation, which is what muscle memory is built on
cons: Large turns need more desk space

pros: Faster turns on a small mousepad
cons: Aim becomes speed-dependent and inconsistent

settings.label: ADS Sensitivity / Uniform Soldier Aiming
settings.note: Set it once so that the same hand movement covers the same on-screen distance at every zoom level, then never touch it again. Not something an auto-tuner should decide for you.

settings.label: Audio Mix / Master Volume
settings.note: Not touched. Worth doing by hand though: set the audio preset to headphones/'War Tapes'-equivalent and pull music down, because footstep direction is information.

settings.label: Music Volume
settings.note: Music masks footsteps and reloads. Competitive players run it at or near zero.

pros: Footsteps, reloads and vehicle audio stop being masked - audio is information
cons: Less atmosphere

pros: More atmospheric
cons: Masks the footsteps and reloads you need to hear

settings.label: Sharpening
settings.note: A contrast-adaptive sharpening pass, most useful paired with an upscaler or a resolution scale below 100%, both of which soften the image. Close to free on GPU time. Unverified: this app's authors have not confirmed BF6's exact menu wording or profile key for it, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand and treat the recommended value as a starting point.

pros: Recovers edge clarity lost to upscaling or a sub-100% resolution scale
Makes distant players easier to pick out against foliage
cons: Over-sharpening haloes edges and can make distant textures shimmer - worse for target ID than it helps

pros: Cleaner, less noisy image, especially paired with TAA
cons: Softer edges, more noticeable if you are running an upscaler below native

settings.label: View / LOD Distance
settings.note: Controls the distance at which meshes drop to lower-detail models and how far out foliage and props draw in. Unlike most settings here, going low is not a clean competitive win: it can make distant enemies pop into view later for you too, not just look worse - which is why esports/competitive keep this at High rather than the usual minimum. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Distant objects and enemies render in detail sooner instead of popping in late
Better information at long sightlines on open maps
cons: Real GPU and CPU cost from extra draw calls and mesh detail at range
Smaller benefit on dense, close-quarters maps

pros: Meaningful GPU/CPU saving, especially on open maps
cons: Distant enemies and objects pop into full detail later, which cuts both ways against an opponent running this higher
More visible LOD popping and foliage draw-in

settings.label: Reflection Quality
settings.note: Screen-space reflections on wet surfaces, glass and water. Mostly cosmetic - it does not hide or reveal players the way vegetation or shadows do - so cutting it is close to a free GPU saving for competitive play. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Convincing reflections on wet ground, glass and water
cons: A real GPU cost for something you are rarely looking directly at in a firefight

pros: Close to a free GPU saving - reflections rarely carry gameplay information
cons: Wet surfaces and glass look flat

settings.label: Weapon Field of View
settings.note: Independent from world Field of View above - this only changes how large your weapon model appears, not how much of the world you see. Free to render either way; purely a preference for how 'zoomed in' the gun feels. Unverified: not confirmed against a real BF6 profile, so it is not written to your profile automatically - set it by hand.

pros: Less of the screen occupied by the weapon model
cons: Some players prefer a low weapon FOV that feels unified with a low world FOV

pros: Gun feels closer and bigger, which some players prefer for weapon feedback
cons: More of the screen is taken up by the viewmodel

unverified_settings_note: A setting marked confidence: 'unverified' is a plausible addition based on common Frostbite/FPS conventions - proposed by BF6 Tuner's own tooling, not sourced from a confirmed BF6 profile dump or menu screenshot. Each one deliberately has no profsave_key, so it is never written to your profile automatically (see database.py/writer.py's 'never invent PROFSAVE keys' rule) - it only ever shows up as a recommendation with reasoning, for you to set by hand and verify. Promote an entry out of 'unverified' by confirming its real menu wording and PROFSAVE key against an actual game install, then add profsave_key and drop the confidence field.

cost_model.units: Values are percent of total GPU or CPU frame time relative to the setting's baseline option, and GB for vram.
cost_model.baseline: The option whose entry is all zeroes. For quality tiers that is normally 'High'.
cost_model.interpolate: Slider settings set interpolate=true; values between the listed anchors are interpolated linearly.
cost_model.caveat: These are modelled magnitudes, not per-machine measurements. They are used to rank changes and estimate direction, and the app says so.
